transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. Um, well, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten really out of hand lately with... well, with eating. I work as a cashier, right? And it's just, you know, you're standing on your feet all day, dealing with customers, scanning things for eight hours straight, and by the time I clock out, my brain is just completely fried. But instead of just going home and having a normal dinner, I've been doing this thing where... well, I keep buying these huge takeout orders. 

And I mean *huge*. Like, I'll go to the drive-thru and order enough burgers, multiple large fries, a whole box of fried chicken, maybe a couple of milkshakes and those little pies they have—honestly, it looks exactly like I'm picking up dinner for an entire family. The people working the window probably think I'm heading home to a wife and three kids or having a party or something. But it's just me. And I won't even wait to get to my house. I'll just sit there, usually right in my car in some parking lot, and I'll eat almost all of it myself before I even go home. It takes a while, and I just sit there surrounded by all these wrappers and bags, and I just... I keep doing it, shift after shift, and I really need to figure out how to stop.
When you're sitting in the car eating all of that food, do you feel like you can't stop yourself or control how much you eat during those moments?

Yeah, exactly. That's exactly what it is. It's like... well, it's like my brain just completely shuts down, you know? Like, I'll be sitting there, the engine is still running, the heater's on, and I've got all these bags spread out on the passenger seat and in my lap. And before I even start, I might think, 'Okay, I'm just going to eat the fries and one burger, and I'll save the rest for tomorrow.' But then... once I take that first bite, it feels like something in me just clicks off. 

It's like I'm on autopilot, but a really destructive kind of autopilot. I'll be chewing, and in the back of my head, there's this voice—my own voice—going, 'Demetrius, stop, man. You don't need any more. You're going to make yourself sick. Just put the burger down.' But my hands... my hands just keep reaching into the bag. It's like they have a mind of their own. I'll finish one thing, crumple up the wrapper, toss it in the back seat, and immediately grab the next box. I don't even really taste it after a certain point. It's just this frantic... needing to get it all in. And I know I should stop, I know I'm full, I know I'm going to regret it, but I just can't make myself stop until every single crumb is gone. It's terrifying, honestly, how little control I have in those moments. It's like I'm watching myself do it from the outside, but I can't hit the brakes.
After you finish eating all that food, do you ever try to make up for it by making yourself vomit, taking laxatives, or exercising a lot more than usual?

No, no, I don't do any of that. I mean, I've honestly thought about it, especially the throwing up part, because when I'm done eating all of that... man, my stomach is stretched so tight it actually physically hurts. Like a sharp pain right under my ribs. But I hate throwing up, I really do, I just can't bring myself to do it. I just sit there feeling like a balloon that's about to pop. 

And as for exercising... man, after standing on one of those cheap anti-fatigue mats at the register for eight hours, scanning heavy bags of dog food and cases of water, my lower back is absolutely screaming. My feet throb. The absolute last thing I'm going to do after a shift like that, especially with all that heavy greasy food sitting in my gut, is go for a run or hit a gym. I don't mess with laxatives or anything like that either. I just... I just suffer through it, I guess. 

I'll finally put the car in drive, head back to my apartment, and I'll walk in feeling so sluggish. I can barely even bend over to unlace my work boots because my stomach is just so painfully full and bloated. So I just kind of kick my shoes off and collapse on the couch, usually not even turning the TV on, just staring at the ceiling in the dark. And I just lay there feeling so heavy, you know? Heavy and just completely disgusted with myself. I'll lie there and tell myself, 'Demetrius, tomorrow you're gonna wake up early, you're gonna go for a long walk, you're gonna burn this off and make things right.' But I never do. I just wake up feeling exhausted and gross, put my uniform back on, go back to the store, and just... wait for the whole cycle to happen all over again. I just absorb it all. I never actually do anything to get rid of it.
Before these episodes of overeating happen, do you usually feel upset, anxious, or down about yourself or your life?

Um... no, not really? I mean, I don't think so. I wouldn't say I'm sitting there feeling super depressed or like, having a panic attack or anything like that right before I hit the drive-thru. It's not like I'm crying at the register or agonizing over my life choices, you know? It's more just... well, it's hard to explain. 

Like I said, I've been on my feet all day. So if you ask me how I feel, it's mostly just this intense, bone-deep exhaustion. You know when you've been listening to the exact same repetitive noises for eight hours straight? The beep, beep, beep of the barcode scanner, the squeaky wheels on the shopping carts, people arguing with me about expired coupons, that terrible corporate pop music they play on a loop over the store speakers... it really, really wears you down. By the time my shift is over and I finally get to punch out, my brain is just static. Just pure white noise. 

I'll walk out through those automatic sliding doors, and I'm walking across the asphalt to my car, digging in my pockets for my keys, and I'm not really thinking about my life or feeling down about myself, honestly. I'm not thinking about my rent or being thirty and still wearing a polyester vest for a living or anything deep like that. I'm just... I don't know, blank? I guess I've never really stopped to analyze my exact mood right in that specific moment before I pull out of the employee lot. I just know the urge for the food hits me. But I don't think there's a specific sadness or anxiety causing it, at least not that I've ever noticed. It's just the end of the day, and I'm completely fried, and then I'm just heading straight for the drive-thru. So yeah, I wouldn't say I'm upset beforehand. I really couldn't tell you if there's an emotion there at all besides just being totally drained.

latest_inference.note: The patient does not engage in compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, laxative use, or excessive exercise after overeating, which rules out F50.0 (Anorexia Nervosa) and F50.9 (Eating Disorder, Unspecified). The presentation is consistent with binge eating disorder (F50.81), characterized by recurrent episodes of eating large quantities of food without compensatory behaviors, and a sense of lack of control during the episodes.
